 Susan Smith, who has served 31 years of a life sentence for drowning her two young sons in 1994, was unanimously denied parole by the South Carolina Board of Paroles and Pardons after a hearing Thursday.
 Smith appeared before South Carolina’s parole board for a second time, 32 years after drowning her two young sons in 1994.
 She was convicted in 1995 of killing her boys – Michael, 3, and Alex, 14 months – by leaving them strapped in their car seats while she let her car roll into a lake and sink.
 At the hearing, Smith testified on her own behalf, saying she was “not the same person” she was 32 years ago.
 “I know that what I did to Michael and Alex is horrible…I have a lot of remorse, and I want to say that I’m very, very sorry…” she said over a video call from prison. “They were innocent children. They did not deserve to die.”
 Her ex-husband David Smith recently told CNN he still finds it hard to understand why she killed their children.
 He spoke against granting her parole at the hearing.
 “I’m here to advocate for Michael and Alex, not for me,” David said. “I’m just here to ask you all to look in your heart and see their father’s pain and his still broken heart, and ask your heart: Is 32 years enough for what she did to Michael and Alex?”

 Kevin Brackett and Tommy Pope, who prosecuted Smith’s case, warned the parole board she could profit from her crimes if released by selling her story to journalists or through social media.
 “If you think this family has been through hell now, imagine every day if you pick up your phone or you turn on your computer, and there’s Susan talking about that,” Pope said.
 Smith initially told police her sons were taken when she was carjacked by a Black man in the city of Union, setting off a nine-day manhunt that made international headlines and cast suspicion on Black residents in the town. The young mother – Smith was 23 at the time – tearfully begged for her sons’ return in images shown around the world.
 Investigators were skeptical of Smith’s story from the start; however, she eventually confessed under questioning.
 Susan Smith wipes away a tear during a parole hearing on November 20, 2024, in Columbia, South Carolina. It was the first parole hearing for Smith. She appeared at the hearing via video. 
 The Island Packet/Tribune News Service/Getty Images 
 The board unanimously denied parole at Smith’s first hearing two years ago after her ex-husband and 14 other witnesses gave emotional statements opposing her release.
 After the board made its announcement Thursday, David said he was grateful.
 “We are very grateful to the parole board for keeping her incarcerated for another two years,” he said. “Thank you for keeping Michael and Alex as the focus point.”
 In South Carolina, eligible inmates generally receive a parole reconsideration every two years after they are first denied.
 Smith’s three decades in prison haven’t been uneventful. She has faced a number of internal disciplinary charges .
 Months before the 2024 parole hearing, Smith was charged with “communicating with a victim and/or witness” through telephone calls with a documentary filmmaker, according to the South Carolina Department of Corrections.
 During her parole hearing, officials noted Smith has had no disciplinary infractions since her 2024 hearing.
 Inmates in South Carolina may receive and send letters but cannot legally communicate with journalists in person or by phone.
 CNN’s Faith Karimi contributed to this report.
 This story has been updated with additional information.
